data.title: BFA Global Investors sets up Asia HQ in Singapore
data.description:
Local investors can now connect with US opportunities.

BFA Global Investors, a US private investment manager, established its Asia headquarters in Singapore on 26 November, after receiving a Capital Markets Services License from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

The headquarters is led by Jonathan Belz, global chief executive officer, and Tina Gill, managing director, Asia.

BFA has built relationships with leading US venture and growth managers for over two decades, with some dating back to 2005. Its direct investments include SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks and Anduril, alongside emerging artificial intelligence firms such as Higgsfield, Groq, Decart and Instinct.

Jonathan Belz has over 20 years of experience in investment banking and private markets, working at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse, across Australia, Hong Kong and the US.

Meanwhile, Tina Gill has more than a decade of investment experience in Singapore, most recently as portfolio manager at an institutionalised Singapore-based family office. Prior to that, she worked at Brookfield Asset Management.

Since its establishment in 2019, BFA has grown to six offices across Australia, Asia and the US, with more than $428.5m (AU$500m) in assets under administration as of 1 October.

"Singapore is where Asia's private wealth is being built and managed and our MAS licence means we can now serve investors directly from the region. It’s the foundation for expanding BFA across Asia as we grow our team and our investor relationships here,” said Belz.

AU$1=SG$0.86 as of 26 November.

data.title: Fraud and scam claims rise 18%, remain top financial dispute
data.description:
Most cases involved compromised credentials and unauthorised bank transactions.

The Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre Ltd (FIDReC) received 1,515 fraud and scam claims in the financial year ending 30 June, up 18% year on year from 1,285, making it the largest claim type for the third consecutive year.

The majority of fraud and scam claims involved compromised credentials and unauthorised transactions on customers’ bank accounts, FIDReC said.

Overall claims across all categories rose 23% to a record 5,344, from 4,355 previously.

Claims relating to financial institutions’ practices and policies increased 37% to 889, from 649. Service standards claims recorded the largest increase, rising 61% to 520 from 323, whilst market conduct claims grew 11% to 432 from 389.

Claims also increased across all categories of financial institutions. Banks, finance companies, and credit bureaus accounted for 2,009 claims, compared with 1,831 previously.

Life and composite insurers recorded 481 claims, up from 323, whilst general and composite insurers saw claims rise to 474 from 297. Capital markets services licensees logged 163 claims, up from 94.

Licensed financial advisers and insurance brokers recorded 104 claims, compared with 84 previously. Claims involving payment service providers jumped to 125 from 17.

data.title: OCBC opens 100-tonne physical gold vault in Singapore
data.description:
It can store roughly around 8,000 large gold bars that weigh 12.4 kilograms each.

OCBC launched a dedicated gold vault in Singapore on 26 November.

The new facility has approximately 100 tonnes of vaulting capacity, equal to roughly 8,000 large gold bars that weigh 12.4 kilograms each.

The facility is expected to support OCBC’s ambitions for a physical gold business, which was launched for its institutional clients and clients of its private banking subsidiary, the Bank of Singapore (BOS).

OCBC said that it has seen growing demand for the services, especially from the Bank of Singapore, as well as from other banks and private banks.

“Interest in physical gold has been strong since our launch, reflecting growing demand from clients seeking secure and Singapore-based solutions in relation to their physical gold needs,” said Kenneth Lai, head of global market at OCBC.

OCBC said that it will continue to explore extending physical gold, as well as other physical gold-linked investment and hedging solutions, to additional segments across the group.

In June 2026, OCBC launched physical gold buy, sell, and custody services to eligible clients.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore recently launched a central bank gold vaulting service and will also offer gold custody accounts to select Singapore-based bullion banks.

data.title: MAS cuts approval time for non-traditional retail funds to three months
data.description:
This is down from the previous six- to 12-month timeline.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has shortened the authorisation process for non-traditional retail funds to three months as it seeks to accommodate new investment products.

Under amendments to the Code on Collective Investment Schemes (CIS Code), funds with innovative features that fall outside existing investment guidelines may now be authorised under a new Non-Traditional Funds Appendix.

The revised framework reduces the initial authorisation process to about three months, compared with six to 12 months previously.

Subsequent funds of the same type can be authorised within three weeks.

MAS will work with industry stakeholders to establish appropriate safeguards whenever a new type of non-traditional fund is proposed.

These may include enhanced disclosure requirements to help retail investors understand the products.

The changes aim to address evolving investor needs and growing industry interest in offering retail funds that support a wider range of investment objectives.

Existing protections for retail investors, including custody and liquidity standards, will remain in place.

MAS said fund managers and distributors must continue to prioritise fair dealing when designing and distributing products to retail investors.

Financial institutions must also provide clear investor education materials to help customers make informed investment decisions.

data.title: Poor governance raises barriers to emerging-market investment
data.description:
GFTN says investors are weighing governance standards, valuations and geopolitical risks.

Weak corporate governance could undermine emerging markets' ability to attract international capital as investors become more selective about valuations, geopolitical risks and exposure to artificial intelligence disruption, according to the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN).

Neil Parekh, group deputy chairman and board director at GFTN, said governance remains a critical consideration for international investors assessing opportunities across multiple jurisdictions.

He explained that poor governance increases the time and resources required to monitor portfolio investments, making such markets less attractive to investors managing diversified portfolios.

"If you get into a jurisdiction with poor governance and a company with poor governance, you're going to spend a disproportionate amount of time," he said.

Beyond governance, geopolitical developments are carrying greater weight in investment decisions as countries and companies reassess their international relationships.

Parekh said investors must also scrutinise ambitious growth projections and valuations, particularly where company forecasts depend on rapid expansion whilst maintaining profit margins.

AI disruption presents another risk, with existing business models potentially facing significant changes as automation advances.

He cited software companies facing investor concerns over AI competition and questioned whether healthcare research businesses could experience similar disruption.

Interest rate volatility and inflation expectations, partly influenced by geopolitical developments and commodity prices, add further uncertainty.

For emerging economies seeking international capital, Parekh emphasised that governance must be accompanied by economic growth, openness to innovation and the capacity to adopt new technologies.

data.title: UOB shifts AI focus from adoption to returns
data.description:
The bank targets 900 million in projected AI value by 2030.

United Overseas Bank (UOB) is shifting its artificial intelligence (AI) strategy towards measurable financial returns, targeting 900 million in projected economic value by 2030 as it moves beyond broad workforce adoption.

Lee Zhu Kuang, managing director and group head of Innovation Group at UOB, said widespread AI use builds workforce capabilities, but targeted automation delivers the business impact.

With more than 30,000 employees using Copilot daily and 90% upskilled in generative AI, UOB is measuring returns through revenue growth, productivity improvements and risk reduction rather than adoption rates alone.

"Adoption is not ROI itself," Lee said, stressing that specific AI initiatives must generate tangible economic value.

The distinction is becoming increasingly important as banks transition from generative AI tools towards agentic systems capable of executing tasks across business operations.

Lee expects these systems to reduce processing times, eliminate operational friction and improve cost efficiency. However, greater autonomy also introduces governance challenges.

He said banks must establish clear boundaries around which decisions AI can recommend, execute independently or escalate for human approval. AI decisions must also remain traceable, explainable and auditable.

"Human accountability, especially on material decisions, should not be delegated to AI," Lee said.

The bank is also adjusting its approach to workforce development as automation takes over repetitive analytical tasks traditionally handled by junior employees.

Lee said AI could help younger employees develop judgment, creativity and business understanding earlier in their careers rather than spend time on routine work.

Looking towards 2027, he expects AI to evolve from a standalone productivity tool into technology that coordinates workflows across banking operations.

Beyond cost reductions, Lee identified more responsive, personalised and resilient banking services as potential sources of competitive advantage.

"Success will not be determined by who deploys the most AI, but it will be determined by who can actually scale trusted AI better," he said.

data.title: Kimly earnings sink 30.4% to $14.3m in second half
data.description:
Full-year net profit dropped 11.6% to $32.5m.

Kimly Limited's profit after tax slumped 30.4% to $14.3m in the second half, following a strong first half, according to its unaudited financial statements.

The decline also pulled its full-year net profit down 11.6% to $32.5m from last year's $36.8m.

The statement, posted on 25 November, showed a flat revenue of $322.5m (+0.1%) year on year (YoY). First-half profit after tax had risen 12.3% to $18.2m, but second-half sales slipped 1.0%.

The group attributed the decline in profit mainly to higher labour costs from increased headcount and wage adjustments.

Revenue is mainly supported by the group's Food Retail Division, albeit falling 2.4% to $178.5m from $182.8m YoY.

This was attributed to weaker revenue from existing food stalls and the closure of six underperforming food stalls in 2025 and 11 food stalls and a restaurant in 2026, partly offset by 12 new stalls opened in each year.

Outlet Management ($133.1m) and Outlet Investment ($10.9m) divisions also contributed more to revenue, with combined revenue up 3.4%, supported by the opening of three coffee shops and one drink stall in 2025 and an additional three coffee shops and a hawker centre this year.

Cost of sales increased by $6.4m to $234.4m. Employee benefits expenses rose $5.9m on increased headcount and wage adjustments under the Progressive Wage Model, and grants under the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme fell $2.7m.

Depreciation of right-of-use assets on outlet leases rose $1.5m, whilst utility and cleaning costs rose $0.5m and $0.2m, partially offset by a $1.6m drop in food ingredient costs.

Gross profit fell 6.4% to $88.0m from $94.1m, with a gross margin of 27.3% against 29.2%. Profit attributable to owners slid 12.2% to $29.2m from $33.3m.

Still, the report said cash flow remains resilient, as operating cash flow rose to $89.4m from $85.3m, and cash to $73.6m from $68.1m. Lease liabilities dropped to $126.4m from $142.8m.

Meanwhile, the group bought a coffee shop property at 12 Haig Road for $11.8m in January, which it said reduces lease renewal risk. It has also applied to transfer its listing from the Catalist board to the Mainboard of the Singapore Exchange.

Kimly proposed a final dividend of $0.01 per share for H2, bringing the annual dividend to $0.02 apiece, unchanged from 2025. The dividend payout ratio is 85.2%

The statements said books close on 5 February 2027.

The final dividend is expected to be paid on or about 15 February 2027, pending approval at Kimly's annual general meeting on or about 27 January.

data.title: Resorts World Sentosa launches two-year AI and robotics trials
data.description:
A driverless vehicle is being used for pastry deliveries.

Resorts World Sentosa (RWS) has launched SYMBIOSIS, a two-year initiative to trial artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and digital solutions across its 49-hectare integrated resort.

The initiative is supported by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Singapore Tourism Board, with trials focused on automating resort operations.

The IMDA will connect RWS with technology partners to trial AI solutions, with plans to extend successful applications to other businesses and industries.

One of the ongoing trials is an autonomous refrigerated vehicle that delivers macarons and pastries from the resort's kitchen to Pierre Hermé.

Meanwhile, RWS plans to train employees to work alongside new technologies and take on higher-value roles.

data.title: Legal certainty key to cross-border trade and investment: CJ Menon
data.description:
He stressed coordination amongst courts and arbitration tribunals. 

Singapore's ability to sustain cross-border trade and investment depends on a legal system that upholds arbitration agreements and prevents repeated litigation across jurisdictions, Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon said on 25 November.

Greater coordination amongst courts, arbitration tribunals, and other legal institutions is needed to resolve international commercial disputes effectively, Menon told the Global Rule of Law Conference.

“But a transnational system cannot function coherently if an issue that has already been conclusively determined between the parties by a competent foreign court can be litigated afresh whenever the dispute resurfaces in another jurisdiction,” he added.

Menon cited several Court of Appeal decisions limiting repeated litigation in Singapore, including the Deutsche Telekom case, where a prior foreign court ruling could preclude further challenges to an arbitration award's validity. 

He also highlighted Singapore's involvement in establishing the Bahrain International Commercial Court, whose appeals may be brought before the International Committee of the Singapore International Commercial Court.

The arrangement could help reduce inconsistencies in commercial laws across jurisdictions and provide greater legal certainty for businesses operating internationally, Menon said.

In addition, Menon linked the government’s anti-corruption framework and enforceability of commercial commitments to its ability to attract foreign investment.

Singapore recorded $197b in foreign direct investment inflows in 2025. It also ranked second globally for absence of corruption and third for regulatory enforcement in the 2026 World Justice Project Rule of Law Index.

data.title: Singapore faces possible US tariffs of up to 20% after trade probe
data.description:
The rate could drop to 10% following a reciprocal trade deal or other negotiations. 

The US proposed imposing tariffs of up to 20% on Singapore goods following an investigation into excess manufacturing capacity and production on 25 November.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) said the rate could be adjusted to 10% if Singapore reaches a reciprocal trade agreement with the US or concludes other negotiations addressing the investigation's findings.

The proposed tariffs are net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods.

The maximum tariff rate is higher than the 18% proposed for Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Cambodia.

The investigations were launched on 11 March, covering 16 economies under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974.

The USTR said it received 1,070 comments and testimony from nearly 140 witnesses across the investigations.

Interested parties have until 5 January 2027 to submit written comments and requests to participate in public hearings, which are scheduled to begin on 25 January.

The USTR said Singapore is amongst 14 economies whose manufacturing-related policies and practices it deemed unreasonable and a burden or restriction on US commerce.

The authority cited industrial plans, financial repression, savings policies that suppress domestic consumption, inadequate labour protections, and financial support for key sectors.

It also cited the republic’s alleged failure to address global excess manufacturing capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies.
